title: Microscopic theory of the field-induced instability of the vortex-free state in superconducting thin-film strips
abstract: In the Pearl--London theory, the edge-barrier-disappearance field of a superconducting thin-film strip depends on an arbitrary short-distance core cutoff because the vortex is treated as a point object. The theory does not determine the cutoff or how it depends on temperature $T$, and therefore cannot determine the $T$ dependence of the instability field. Here we formulate the microscopic stability problem directly for the vortex-free superconducting state. This removes the core-cutoff ambiguity and determines the instability field $B_s$ over the full temperature range and across all width regimes considered here. For a homogeneous dirty strip with negligible self-field, three width regimes occur. For $W<W_1(T)$, superconductivity disappears continuously into the normal state through a one-dimensional (1D) instability. For $W_1(T)<W<W_2(T)$, an edge-selective two-dimensional (2D) long-wavelength mode becomes unstable. For $W>W_2(T)$, the critical wave number is finite and the unstable mode is localized near an edge. In the wide-strip limit, $B_s\propto1/W$, recovering the Pearl--London scaling. In sufficiently narrow strips, however, the Pearl--London edge-barrier picture fails qualitatively.
summary: This paper develops a microscopic theory to accurately predict when a vortex-free superconducting thin film becomes unstable due to an applied magnetic field. By formulating the stability problem directly, it resolves ambiguities present in older models and maps out three distinct physical regimes based on the strip's width relative to characteristic lengths. The work is significant for understanding superconductivity in confined geometries.
main_problem: To microscopically determine the field-induced instability of the vortex-free state in superconducting thin-film strips, overcoming ambiguities found in older theories.
main_result: The theory establishes three distinct width regimes for instability: 1D instability, edge-selective 2D mode instability, and localized modes. It shows that for narrow strips, the classical Pearl–London picture fails qualitatively.
method: Stability is analyzed by examining the quadratic variation of the Gibbs free energy functional using Usadel theory formalism, considering both 1D and 2D perturbations.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a homogeneous dirty superconducting thin-film strip subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field. The analysis uses theoretical tools derived from superconductivity theory (Usadel equations).
key_observables: Instability field ($B_s$), critical wave number ($k^*$), and the order parameter amplitude.
important_parameters: Strip width ($W$), temperature ($T$), and magnetic field strength ($B$). The analysis identifies crossover widths $W_1(T)$ and $W_2(T)$.
main_assumptions: The calculations assume a homogeneous strip, negligible self-field effects, and no applied transport current.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the width dependence of $B_s$ at $T=0$, marking the three instability regimes. Figure 2 shows how these critical fields change with temperature.
paper_structure: The paper develops the stability analysis by first considering 1D perturbations, then extending to 2D modes using Fourier decomposition for longitudinal wave numbers ($k$). The results are synthesized to define $B_s$ as the minimum instability field across all considered modes and regimes.
why_interesting: While focused on superconductivity, the rigorous stability analysis of a macroscopic quantum state (the superconducting order parameter) under external fields provides valuable techniques for analyzing phase transitions in complex many-body systems relevant to open quantum systems.
